analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal sugar price supports, marketing allotments, and sugar import quotas, aiming for lower sugar prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 35 House members from both parties, was sent to the House Agriculture Committee, then to a subcommittee in May 2011, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would dismantle the federal sugar program, which supports domestic sugar prices through loans to growers, limits on how much sugar each producer can sell, and tight limits on sugar imports. It would replace the import limits with a requirement that the Agriculture Department set quotas high enough to keep an adequate supply of sugar in the United States at reasonable prices, and it would also end a program that buys surplus sugar to turn into bioenergy. Its effect would be to bring U.S. sugar prices closer to world prices, which are roughly half the U.S. price [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy sugar and any food made with it — candy, baked goods, cereal, soft drinks — would pay less. Food manufacturers that use sugar as a main ingredient would see their largest input cost fall, which is why some candy makers have moved production to countries with cheaper sugar. Foreign sugar exporters would gain access to a larger share of the U.S. market [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar price support program, under which the government lends growers money at rates pegged to a support price for their sugar [S2][S3].
Repeals sugar marketing allotments, which divide the domestic market among growers and processors and restrict how much each can sell [S2][S3].

Replaces the fixed sugar import quota system with a requirement that the Secretary of Agriculture set tariff-rate quotas at the level needed to ensure an adequate supply of sugar at reasonable prices in the United States [S2][S3].
Repeals the feedstock flexibility program, which buys surplus domestic sugar and gives it to bioenergy producers, and repeals related sugar storage loans and payments [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Domestic sugar growers — sugarcane growers concentrated in Florida, Louisiana, Hawaii and Texas, and sugar beet growers across the upper Midwest and Northwest — along with the mills and refiners that process their crops. They would lose guaranteed support prices, guaranteed market shares, and protection from lower-priced imports, and many would face lower prices for their crops.

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes domestic sugar growers to world prices, which have historically fallen below U.S. production costs at times; growers argue that without protection, foreign sugar sold by state-trading enterprises at lower prices would shrink or end domestic sugar production, leaving the country dependent on imports [S3].

Regions built around cane and beet processing — including parts of Minnesota, North Dakota, Idaho, Florida and Louisiana — would bear job losses if processing capacity closed, a cost borne locally even while consumers nationwide saved a small amount on groceries.

Savings per household would be real but modest: sugar is a small share of grocery spending, so the average family gains little per year even as the price gap between U.S. and world sugar is roughly a factor of two.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The economics favor consumers overall: the U.S. sugar program keeps domestic sugar prices far above world prices, and the costs are spread across every household in the form of higher food prices while the benefits go to a few thousand farms and processors. The serious costs of repeal would fall on the beet and cane regions that lose production and processing jobs, and the bill does not provide any transition for them. On balance it would transfer income from consumers to their own grocery budgets at the expense of a small, protected industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then to its subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management in May 2011, and no markup, report, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Pitts (R-PA) introduced the bill on April 6, 2011 with Rep. Danny Davis (D-IL) as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture [S5].
On May 11, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management, where it remained with no further action [S5].
The bill attracted 34 cosponsors, 25 Republicans and 9 Democrats, but was never brought up for a vote in committee or on the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic sugar growers and processors are better off because the bill died: the price supports, marketing allotments, and import quotas that keep U.S. sugar prices near double world prices remained in place, and consumers continued to pay the difference at the grocery store.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but limited: 25 Republicans and 9 Democrats signed on, and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote showing the actual breakdown.

industries.industry: U.S. sugar cane and beet growers and processors
industries.note: The federal sugar program — price support loans, marketing allotments limiting how much each producer can sell, and tight import quotas — keeps U.S. sugar prices near double world prices, transferring roughly a billion dollars a year from consumers to a few thousand farms and mills. Repealing it removes that guaranteed income and exposes growers to world prices, which is precisely why the industry works so hard to keep the program.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baking, cereal, beverages)
industries.note: Sugar is a major input cost for these manufacturers, and the current program's high prices have pushed some candy and food production to Mexico and Canada. Cheaper sugar would lower their costs and, the bill's logic runs, allow some production and jobs to return to the U.S.
The feedstock flexibility program buys surplus sugar and transfers it to bioenergy producers, creating a small guaranteed outlet and payment; the bill repeals it, ending that subsidy.
Replacing fixed import quotas with a mandate to set tariff-rate quotas at levels ensuring an adequate supply at reasonable prices would open a larger share of the U.S. market to foreign sugar.
